https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-k.text: A Russian drone strike killed at least 27 people near the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday morning. The drone hit a warehouse in the village of Myla, near Kyiv, Zelenskyy said . Residential buildings near the warehouse, including a care home for elderly people and people with disabilities, suffered “significant damage,” he said. More than 370 people have been evacuated and emergency services are continuing work, Zelenskyy said. Advertisement Advertisement The warehouse appears to have been storing ammunition; Zelenskyy referred to a detonation after the drone strikes, and to a police investigation into why ordnance was stored close to residential properties, which is prohibited. Criminal proceedings on charges of negligence have also begun. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” he said. Russia is bombarding Kyiv with “virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones,” Zelenskyy added. In a separate video address Friday evening, he admitted Ukraine needs to “significantly accelerate” production of interceptors capable of taking down the Iranian-designed, jet-powered Shahed drones. In response to Russia’s increased attacks, Ukraine plans to launch 1,000 long-range drones into Russia every day, up from a current average of 300. There “must be more” strikes, Zelenskyy said Friday night. Kyiv’s use of long-range drones — striking deep into Russia, disrupting its economy, logistics and bringing the reality of the war to ordinary Russians previously shielded from it — has in recent months improved Ukraine’s position in the conflict. One Ukrainian commander has described them as “our most important card in this war.” While noting Kyiv's priority is to strengthen defenses against jet-powered drones, sending more long-range drones into Russia will make it “feel even more responsible for its choice to continue this war,” Zelenskyy said Friday night. In the same address, he also pointed to signs that Russia’s economy is ailing, including the fact that it is now importing gasoline , an unusual step for one of the world's largest oil exporters. Zelenskyy also said American representatives briefed Ukraine on the recent unexpected visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who warned Russian officials not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for the "necessary tone of the conversation with Russia." Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/.text: NATO jets shoot down drone in Romanian airspace Aug. 16 (UPI) -- NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Romania's airspace without authorization, the Romanian defense minister said Sunday. Radu Miruța said two Spanish F-18 jets were scrambled in response to the drone entering Romanian airspace at 4:44 a.m. Sunday near the border with Moldova. "At 5:01 [a.m.], the drone was intercepted and destroyed between the localities of Bǎleni and Cudalbi, in Galați County, in an unpopulated area," the defense minister said in a post on X . "Romania is defending its airspace, and our allies are standing with us. Vigilance, rapid response, and allied solidarity - these are the concrete guarantees of our security." Romanian officials did not confirm the country of origin of the drone, but it was one of multiple incursions into the country's airspace in recent weeks, Euronews reported. On July 26, Miruța said a Romanian F-16 shot down a Russian drone that entered Romanian airspace near the delta of the Danube River in the Black Sea. Two days before, Romania shot down another drone that was found to be the type Russia has used in its invasion of Ukraine. On Thursday, Spanish F-18s were also scrambled after an object was spotted in Romanian airspace near the Ukrainian border. It spent 12 minutes in Romanian airspace before moving into Ukraine. https://www.dw.com/en/czech-pm-andrej-ba.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NCRe Babis announced on Monday that the Czech state will run a deficit of 386 billion crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion) next year Image: Michaela Rihova/CTK/picture alliance Advertisement The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO , demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said. The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising. Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania , has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis , whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington. While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases. US Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker (pictured here in Iowa earlier this month) has made the US position clear to Prague: Czechia 'must remain committed to increasing defense spending' Image: Tim Evans/REUTERS That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row. Warnings of a growing threat Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question. A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood. Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies. Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack. Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB). Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow. The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing. However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action. Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year. Prague's priorities Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22. The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion). While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities. The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure. "The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system." That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees . "None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes. Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. 'We don't want World War III' The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine. Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace. "We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict. It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media. The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views. Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget. "A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions." Strategic understanding The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel. Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?" However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target. "Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW. However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Shark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters View image in fullscreen Shark in the canal during operation to guide it out in Busan, South Korea, on Wednesday. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters South Korea Shark trapped for a month in South Korean canal is finally freed Bukang-i successfully guided out after month in which it drew 1.6m visitors and was watched over by YouTubers Raphael Rashid in Seoul Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.41 EDT First published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In South Korea , they call them jagyeongdan , a word whose meaning sits somewhere between vigilante group and neighbourhood watch. Each night they put on hi-vis vests, picked up their selfie sticks and gathered around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: a stranded shark affectionately known as Bukang-i. On Wednesday, after more than a month in the canal and at the third attempt, the shark was successfully guided out, South Korea’s oceans ministry said. Officials expect her to move into open water in time. For the month that she was stranded, the group of self-appointed guardians took turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal. Most are YouTubers who livestreamed the waterway, where the shark became a national celebrity. They stayed up through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times. View image in fullscreen (Left to right) The YouTubers Kim Jong-hwan, Choi Won-jin and Na Tae-soo, who have been keeping watch over the trapped shark in Busan Composite: Supplied/ Yonhap News Agency “They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” said Choi Won-jin , one of the shark’s protectors. He would arrive as the lights went out along the canal and wait for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”. The shark had been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark was one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors came to see her, the city said, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday. View image in fullscreen Visitors watching the shark trapped in a waterway in the south-eastern port city of Busan. Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty Images Authorities had twice tried to guide her back out to sea and failed. Until she left, the shark remained in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrolled the canal’s park to check everything was in order, ate snacks as the night went by, and shared their grievances on air about the behaviour they witnessed. “We’re ordinary members of the public,” said Choi, who has had a YouTube channel for 10 years and covers trending issues in South Korea. “So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.” “Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” said one of them, a YouTuber who lived nearby and went by the name Na Tae-soo . Most people complied, he said. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.” View image in fullscreen Crowds flocked to the waterfront park in Busan to see the shark. Photograph: Yonhap/EPA His footage captured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch was likely to have startled the shark into injury. Korean media reported that 105 officials from seven agencies watched over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputed this, saying that after dark it was almost up to him and the others. The waterfront was closed to the public from midnight until 5am, a restriction the YouTubers said was impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water. Nobody saw the shark feed, though experts said feeding could happen in an instant and sharks her size did not need to eat often. Further attempts to free the shark had been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her. Cooler water had been expected to prompt her to move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute said. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival would become precarious. Busan city officials had expected the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November. View image in fullscreen This aerial photo taken on 29 September shows South Korean coastguard boats spraying water in an attempt to guide the shark back to the sea. Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty Images The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on. The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorative soju , a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October. None of the shark’s guardians thought she should be forced out. Choi said the city should protect her where she was until she left of her own accord. Kim Jong-hwan , who runs a small business, kept watch by day as well and livestreamed her almost every day. “I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he said. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.” “She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim said. “If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.” Explore more on these topics South Korea Sharks Marine life Wildlife Animals Asia Pacific news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light
